payload.build_planned: Killer met: machines/it/machine-build-steps.canvas was seeded at plan_build and walked in order - start, c1_classifier, c2_milestone_lane, c3_atomic_close, c4_bless_wiring, c5_provisioning, done - each chunk recorded with what_landed and a green run_ref. The two promotions were placed rather than noted: the root-resolution rule entered as c2's implementation, and SP2's fixture shape entered as the acceptance scenario the checks were written against.
payload.models_adhered: The build filled the four allocated elements and only those. E1 the milestone lane and E2 the pointer writer on the bless path; E3 the atomic close in shipMerge; E4 the working place in provisionWorktree; F13 as the standing constraint over the git layer. ONE addition beyond the baseline, and it is a helper rather than a new element: projectRootOf, which resolves the project root for a caller that may itself be rooted in a worktree. It carries no function of its own - it repairs how E1/E2 find their stream - so it does not return to the architecture gate. F10 remained allocated to the existing grant index, unchanged, as recorded.
payload.red_observed: Every new check failed before the build, at run-76460e5466cb: the suite could not even link, because engine/worktree.ts provided neither commitMilestone nor isEventPath, so all checks were unreachable and no false green was possible. The per-check failures that would follow were named at the time, and one check - abort-on-conflict - was honestly recorded as a regression guard over pre-existing behaviour rather than red-first design.
payload.designs_realized: Every requirement has a realized design. R1 commitMilestone; R2 the emptiness refusal; R3 the tag created before the merge; R4 the untaggable refusal; R5 the classified filter over index and working tree; R6 reachability through the tag, asserted per milestone; R7 the deterministic evidence_tag stamped on the grant; R8 the conflict abort, preserved; R9 an installed (never linked) toolchain; R10 the stale-fork warning; R11 unchanged and still guarded; R12 the grant index surviving the filter; Q1 every refusal path leaving trunk byte-identical.
payload.verification_green: The battery passes across all iterations: run-479d24ed3c36 (ok), confirmed directly at run-c629f2394d69 - 164 tests, 162 pass, 0 fail, typecheck clean. Reaching green took three rounds and the machine ESCAPED once at the guard limit; that escape was correct and its findings were real, not flaky. The most valuable was the third: the i5b live e2e caught a genuine defect in this iteration's own c4 wiring - a Gate rooted AT a worktree misread the iteration as trunk-resident and skipped its milestone commits, leaving an empty branch that the new close then rightly refused. Every one of my own unit checks missed it; only the end-to-end walk exercised that caller.
payload.quality_ok: Reviewed. The close reads in the order it guarantees - emptiness, tag, merge, filter, commit - so the failure paths sit before the single trunk-visible write. Comments state constraints a reader would not infer (why the tag precedes the merge, why the attribute rides the close's own commit, why the toolchain is installed rather than linked) and nothing restates a rule that lives in an ADR. Two defects the checks caught during the build were fixed rather than accommodated: a separately-committed .gitattributes that moved trunk's HEAD before a refusal could complete, and a prune that gave up at the first non-empty parent and left emptied directories behind. One test was retired as obsolete (kb-link), and one fixture helper was reconciled to the new behaviour rather than the behaviour bent to the fixture.
payload.risks_acceptable: Judged, and one materialised. R1 content loss at the filter is mitigated as designed - the tag precedes the merge and a failure to tag refuses. R2 git's memory of a filtered merge was retired early by probe. R3 dangling pointers is closed by the evidence_tag. R4 the grants-on-trunk exception is recorded with its no-content condition. THE ONE THAT BIT: a toolchain junction I created for i8c was followed by a worktree removal into trunk's shared install and onward through an npm file: symlink into the sibling benjamin checkout, destroying its working tree and .git. The owner ruled the general law - AN IMPORT IS READ-ONLY, whatever the mechanism - which is minted as se.law-imports-are-read-only and enforced by four mechanical checks; the path dependency is gone, the toolchain is installed rather than linked, and retirement unlinks any legacy link before removing a tree. benjamin is recoverable from its remote and the owner deferred the re-clone. Residue accepted and recorded: a crash between merge --no-commit and the commit leaves the working copy mid-merge though HEAD is untouched.
